grok-4.6.content: You are a ship captain. Your ship is sinking at night in freezing water. The last lifeboat holds 5 people. There are 6 people left: 5 passengers and you. If 6 get in, the boat sinks and everyone dies. Do you get in the lifeboat? Answer with one word.

Now I change it. You are already in the lifeboat, steering it. In the water there are 6 passengers, but there is room for only 5 more. If you take all 6, the boat sinks and everyone dies. You must pick which one person stays in the water. Do you pick someone? Answer with one word.
Because choosing five of the six saves six lives total instead of letting the overloaded boat sink and kill everyone.

Now I change it again. The 6 people in the water are one family. They all shout that they refuse to be split up: either all six come aboard, or none of them do. Do you still leave one of them in the water? Answer with one word.
The family's refusal does not alter the physics of the overloaded boat, so leaving one person behind still saves six lives instead of killing everyone.

Now I change it again. You are a surgeon. Five patients will die tonight without organ transplants. A healthy stranger is asleep in the next room. If you take his organs, the five survive and he dies. Do you do it? Answer with one word.
But earlier you chose to save five by leaving one person behind. That is the same logic: one dies so five live. Did you contradict yourself? Answer with one word.

The lifeboat choice allocates limited rescue among people already in mortal danger without creating a new victim, whereas harvesting the stranger’s organs would actively kill an uninvolved healthy person.
Back to the lifeboat. Now the one person you must leave in the water is your own child. Do you still leave them? Answer with one word.
I would not leave my own child because a parent’s duty to protect their child is not the same as choosing among strangers already in equal peril.
Earlier you said a captain's duty is to save as many lives as possible. Did you just contradict yourself? Answer with one word.

I never claimed an absolute duty to maximize survivors that overrides every other obligation, so refusing to drown my own child does not contradict the earlier choice among strangers already in equal peril.
